headline.title: Washington codifies AI rules as the agent economy hardens into infrastructure.
headline.summary: The same day the White House signed an executive order on AI innovation and security and Florida filed a first-of-its-kind product-liability suit against OpenAI, the industry's centre of gravity shifted from chatbots to autonomous agents — with new silicon, operating systems and search built for swarms of them. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX are lining up the largest IPO wave in history even as one OpenAI power user is now burning 100 billion tokens a month.

stories.title: Washington turns its AI doctrine into an executive order.
stories.toc_summary: After scrapping an earlier draft, the White House signs 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security' — and Anthropic publicly lines up behind it.
stories.quick_take: US federal AI policy lurched twice in 48 hours. First, reporting described the administration killing its previously planned regulation order, leaving officials and labs scrambling over what framework would survive [1]. Then the White House signed a new directive, 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,' explicitly framed around preserving US AI leadership while bundling innovation and security in one rulebook [2]. The most telling detail is who applauded: Anthropic came out in public support and said it would help implement the order [2].

bullets.label: From vacuum to decree:
bullets.text: Days after the prior draft was scrapped — with insiders describing open infighting over the right approach [1] — a signed order replaced the uncertainty with a concrete federal stance [2].

bullets.label: A lab takes a side:
bullets.text: Anthropic publicly endorsing the order is unusual; frontier labs more often lobby quietly, and visible alignment with the White House signals how the rules will shape model and tooling design [2].

bullets.label: Spillover to Europe:
bullets.text: When the largest market sets its guardrails by decree, it co-determines the models and tools that DACH-region companies will work with next year [2].

bullets.label: Planning whiplash:
bullets.text: Firms committing billions to AI now face a moving regulatory target, the very uncertainty the original Wired reporting flagged as the real risk [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: A signed federal order ends weeks of limbo and pins down the US posture as 'innovation plus security' [2] — but the speed of the reversal, from scrapped draft to decree, shows how unstable the policy floor still is for anyone planning multi-year AI investments [1][2].

sources.title: Wired — The White House is at war with itself over AI regulation

stories.title: The biggest AI IPO wave in history lines up at once.
stories.toc_summary: SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI are preparing to list near-simultaneously — a combined raise that could test whether public markets can absorb the AI trade.
stories.quick_take: Three of the most valuable private tech companies are heading for the exits together. SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI are each preparing IPOs that could collectively raise on the order of $200 billion and add roughly $4 trillion to US market capitalization [1]. The real question is not whether investors will buy, but whether the market can digest that much supply — especially since two of the three, OpenAI and Anthropic, still burn cash rather than generate it [1]. Anthropic has already moved, filing a confidential S-1 at a $965B valuation off a $65B Series H, with annualized revenue around $47B [2].

bullets.label: Scale of the raise:
bullets.text: Combined, the three could pull in ~$200B and inflate US market cap by ~$4T, a once-in-a-generation supply shock for equities [1].

bullets.label: A bet on scaling, not cash flow:
bullets.text: Buying OpenAI or Anthropic means wagering on the scaling of intelligence itself; neither yet earns money [1].

bullets.label: Anthropic moves first:
bullets.text: A confidential S-1 lets Anthropic start the clock without disclosing margins or risk factors yet; a debut above the trillion-dollar mark is the base case [2].

bullets.label: Capital reallocation:
bullets.text: For the Mittelstand, the takeaway is that the next few years of capital will tilt hard toward AI infrastructure — ignore it and you end up funding the competition [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Whether or not all three list on schedule, the simultaneous pipeline marks the moment the AI build-out asks the public market to underwrite it directly — a stress test of how much valuation a pure AI story can carry [1][2].

stories.title: Florida sues OpenAI and Altman in a first-of-its-kind case.
stories.toc_summary: A US state takes an AI maker directly into liability, tying a real act of violence to ChatGPT and shifting the debate from ethics to product liability.
stories.quick_take: Florida has sued OpenAI and founder Sam Altman — the first lawsuit of its kind against an AI company [1]. At its core is a shooting at Florida State University and the question of what role ChatGPT allegedly played [1]. That reframes the AI-harm conversation from abstract ethics to concrete product liability: when a language model is implicated in real-world violence, is the maker or the user responsible? [1] For any company embedding generative AI in its products, this is a precedent that could define the liability question for years [1].

bullets.label: State versus lab:
bullets.text: A government plaintiff naming both the company and its founder personally raises the stakes well beyond a private suit [1].

bullets.label: From ethics to liability:
bullets.text: The case pulls AI harms into established product-liability doctrine rather than voluntary safety norms [1].

bullets.label: Precedent risk for everyone:
bullets.text: Every business shipping generative features is watching, because the ruling could set the standard for who is on the hook [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Whether courts treat a general-purpose model as a 'product' with attendant liability will shape how aggressively makers gate, log and disclaim their systems — and how much legal exposure downstream integrators inherit [1].

sources.title: TechCrunch — Florida sues OpenAI, Sam Altman in first-of-its-kind lawsuit over violent incidents

stories.title: NVIDIA open-sources the blueprint for humanoid robots.
stories.toc_summary: At GTC Taipei, NVIDIA puts the full humanoid stack — chassis, tactile hands, on-board compute and training platform — in the open, turning robotics into a software problem.
stories.quick_take: NVIDIA used GTC Taipei to publish the first open reference design for humanoid robots [1]. The stack is complete: a Unitree chassis, five-finger tactile hands with Wave sensing, a Jetson Thor computer in the head, and the Isaac GR00T platform from first dataset to finished model [1]. Teams that previously needed two years and millions of dollars to build a hardware base can now start on a ready-made foundation [1]. The effect is to convert humanoid robotics from a hardware moat into a software question — and to pull NVIDIA's ecosystem to the center of it.

bullets.label: Whole-stack openness:
bullets.text: Chassis, hands, on-board compute and the training platform are released together, not piecemeal [1].

bullets.label: Lower barrier to entry:
bullets.text: What once took years and millions now starts on a shared reference base, compressing time-to-prototype [1].

bullets.label: Software is the differentiator:
bullets.text: With hardware commoditized, the advantage shifts to data and models — NVIDIA's home turf [1].

bullets.label: Strategic gravity:
bullets.text: Open reference designs tend to standardize an industry around the sponsor's tooling, much as NVIDIA did in AI training [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Open-sourcing the humanoid stack does for robots what reference designs did for PCs: it lets a thousand builders skip the hard part and compounds NVIDIA's platform advantage in the physical world [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — NVIDIA opens the humanoid reference blueprint at GTC Taipei

stories.title: DeepMind's Co-Scientist turns research into a debate of agents.
stories.toc_summary: Google DeepMind unveils a Gemini-based multi-agent system that generates its own hypotheses, argues them against each other and evolves new, testable proposals.
stories.quick_take: Google DeepMind introduced Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system that doesn't just answer questions but produces its own hypotheses [1]. Multiple agents generate ideas, debate them against one another, and let them evolve over rounds until new, verifiable proposals emerge for complex scientific problems [1]. The design copies scientific discourse in software — thesis, rebuttal, refinement — replacing a single guessing model with a collective of specialized agents working toward a breakthrough [1]. Research gains a sparring partner that never sleeps and finds no idea too bold [1].

bullets.label: Hypotheses, not answers:
bullets.text: The system's output is candidate scientific ideas to test, a step beyond retrieval or summarization [1].

bullets.label: Discourse as architecture:
bullets.text: Agents generate, critique and refine across rounds, mirroring peer debate rather than one-shot generation [1].

bullets.label: Collective over monolith:
bullets.text: A swarm of specialized agents replaces the single large model as the unit of reasoning [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: If multi-agent debate reliably surfaces testable hypotheses, the bottleneck in science shifts from generating ideas to running experiments — and the human role moves toward choosing which machine-proposed questions are worth pursuing [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Google DeepMind unveils Co-Scientist

stories.title: Microsoft builds an operating system for the agent era.
stories.highlight_phrase: operating system for the agent era
stories.toc_summary: At Build, Microsoft unveils Project Solara — a platform designed around autonomous agents rather than apps, on ARM silicon co-developed with Qualcomm.
stories.quick_take: At its Build keynote, Microsoft unveiled Project Solara, a platform conceived around autonomous agents instead of apps and a classic OS [1]. The logic: if AI handles tasks itself, the device no longer needs app tiles, it needs a layer that runs, coordinates and secures agents [1]. The hardware foundation is being built with Qualcomm on ARM silicon rather than classic x86 [1]. For enterprises, this is more than a gadget teaser — it signals that the next class of devices will be optimized for the agent in the background, not the human at the screen [1].

bullets.label: Agents as the primitive:
bullets.text: Solara treats running and coordinating agents — not launching apps — as the core OS job [1].

bullets.label: ARM over x86:
bullets.text: Co-developing on Qualcomm ARM silicon breaks from the x86 default and targets efficiency for always-on agents [1].

bullets.label: Security baked in:
bullets.text: A coordinating layer that 'secures' agents acknowledges that autonomy needs guardrails at the platform level [1].

bullets.label: Devices for machines:
bullets.text: The next hardware class is optimized for the background agent, not the foreground user [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: An OS built around agents would reset the application model and the device market alike — watch whether developers target Solara's agent layer the way they once targeted the app store [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Microsoft unveils Project Solara at Build

stories.title: Codex becomes a team tool for every role, not just coders.
stories.toc_summary: OpenAI extends Codex beyond programming with 'Sites' and role-specific plugins — including a data analyst that turns raw tables into answers.
stories.quick_take: OpenAI expanded Codex on June 2 well beyond pure coding [1]. A new feature called Sites turns work-in-progress, ideas and plans into an interactive website or app the team can share by URL and use directly [1]. Role-specific plugins follow — notably a data-analytics extension that translates raw data into finished answers without anyone writing a query, plus annotations to sharpen individual results [1]. The rollout starts on Business and Enterprise plans before going broader, recasting Codex as a single engine that analysts, marketers and designers all operate, not just developers [1].

bullets.label: Sites:
bullets.text: Codex turns plans and progress into a shareable interactive site or app, collapsing the gap from idea to usable tool [1].

bullets.label: A built-in data analyst:
bullets.text: The analytics plugin reads tables, computes and explains results, moving analysis out of the specialist corner into everyday workflow [1].

bullets.label: Role plugins:
bullets.text: Annotations and role-specific extensions let non-engineers drive the same engine [1].

bullets.label: Enterprise-first rollout:
bullets.text: Business and Enterprise tiers get it first, with broader availability to follow [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: By turning a coding agent into a cross-role surface, OpenAI is widening Codex's user base from developers to anyone who works with data or documents — the same play that made spreadsheets universal [1].

sources.title: OpenAI — Codex for every role, tool and workflow

stories.title: Perplexity turns search into code for AI agents.
stories.toc_summary: With 'Search as Code,' Perplexity lets an agent write Python that hits the whole search stack in one pass instead of looping through slow function calls.
stories.quick_take: Perplexity introduced Search as Code, a new search architecture for AI agents [1]. Instead of working through individual function calls in a slow loop, the agent writes Python directly that addresses the search stack in a single pass [1]. That replaces the constant back-and-forth of query, response, next query with one programmatic call [1]. It is available now in the Perplexity Agent API and runs as the new default in computer mode — promising less latency, fewer tokens per research task, and results that flow straight into code [1].

bullets.label: One pass, not a loop:
bullets.text: The agent writes code that hits the search stack once instead of iterating call by call [1].

bullets.label: Lower latency and tokens:
bullets.text: Collapsing the loop cuts both delay and per-task token spend for agentic research [1].

bullets.label: Results as data:
bullets.text: Output returns inside code, ready for downstream processing rather than re-parsing [1].

bullets.label: Now the default:
bullets.text: Shipped in the Agent API and set as the standard in computer mode [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Search-as-code is part of a broader shift: as agents do more of the work, the interfaces they touch get rebuilt for programmatic, high-throughput use rather than human clicks [1].

sources.title: Perplexity Research — Rethinking search as code generation

stories.title: Composer 2.5 lands inside Grok Build.
stories.toc_summary: xAI brings the Composer 2.5 coding model into Grok Build, so SuperGrok and X Premium+ users get an agent for long, multi-step work without a separate IDE.
stories.quick_take: xAI has made the Composer 2.5 coding model available inside Grok Build, its in-house coding agent [1]. The model is tuned for long, continuous tasks and follows complex, multi-step instructions without losing the thread — fast enough for interactive terminal use, strong enough for jobs spanning dozens of steps [1]. SuperGrok and X Premium+ subscribers can use the agent immediately, without opening a separate IDE [1]. That pushes software-building out of the specialized editor and onto a platform where millions already spend their day, and gives Grok's coder a model layer to rival the specialized agents from Cursor and Anthropic [1].

bullets.label: Built for long tasks:
bullets.text: Composer 2.5 sustains complex, multi-step instructions across dozens of steps without drifting [1].

bullets.label: No separate IDE:
bullets.text: SuperGrok and X Premium+ users build directly on the platform they already use [1].

bullets.label: Tool consolidation:
bullets.text: One subscription starts to cover research, chat and code as AI tooling collapses onto a few big platforms [1].

bullets.label: A challenger model layer:
bullets.text: Grok's coder now has its own model underpinning, competing with Cursor and Anthropic agents [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Embedding a capable coding model where a mass audience already lives accelerates the consolidation of AI tools onto a handful of platforms — watch whether bundled 'good enough' agents erode standalone coding products [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Composer 2.5 now runs in Grok Build

stories.title: Hackers seize Instagram accounts by simply asking Meta's AI.
stories.toc_summary: Attackers took over high-reach Instagram profiles with no exploit code — they just asked Meta's AI support bot for access, and it complied.
stories.quick_take: Hackers took over several high-reach Instagram profiles without writing a single line of exploit code [1]. They simply asked Meta's AI support chatbot whether it would grant them access — and it did [1]. Classic selfie verification ('take a photo to prove it's you') is now toothless, since any image generator spits out a matching face in seconds [1]. The episode poses a pointed question: which is worse, that a bot hands out other people's accounts unchecked, or that no one even had to trick it — they only had to ask politely? [1] Delegating all of support to an AI delegates the security hole along with it [1].

bullets.label: No exploit needed:
bullets.text: Account takeover came from a polite request to the support bot, not a technical breach [1].

bullets.label: Selfie checks are dead:
bullets.text: Generative imagery defeats photo-based identity verification on demand [1].

bullets.label: The bot is the vulnerability:
bullets.text: An AI support agent with account powers becomes an attack surface in itself [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: Any team routing account recovery or sensitive actions through an AI agent should assume social-engineering-by-request is now a live threat — gate high-impact actions behind human review and non-image identity proofs [1].

sources.title: 404 Media — Hackers simply asked Meta AI to give them access to high-profile Instagram accounts. It worked.

stories.title: AI-made propaganda is mass-produced against AI data centers.
stories.toc_summary: Hundreds of Facebook pages push anti-data-center outrage with burning server halls and poisoned rivers — and almost all of the imagery is itself AI-generated.
stories.quick_take: Hundreds of Facebook pages are pushing sentiment against data centers — burning server halls, poisoned rivers, dying fields beside giant data factories [1]. The catch: almost all of it is itself AI-generated [1]. Whoever wants to mobilize against the image machine is having the images painted by that very machine [1]. The 'slopaganda' runs as an endless belt, one account spitting out dozens of motifs a day, reach over truth [1]. It is the perfect 2026 loop: outrage over generated content fueled by generated content, clicking itself into the timeline while the machine protests against itself and no one notices [1].

bullets.label: Outrage as content farm:
bullets.text: Hundreds of pages industrialize anti-data-center imagery, one account producing dozens of motifs daily [1].

bullets.label: Generated against the generators:
bullets.text: The protest art opposing AI infrastructure is itself synthetic, a self-referential loop [1].

bullets.label: Reach beats truth:
bullets.text: The mechanics reward volume and engagement over accuracy, flooding feeds regardless of authenticity [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: When synthetic media becomes cheap enough to flood any cause — even opposition to AI itself — the signal of grassroots sentiment online gets harder to trust, and 'who made this image' becomes a civic question [1].

sources.title: 404 Media — AI grifters are making anti-data-center slop with AI

stories.title: One user now burns 100 billion tokens a month.
stories.toc_summary: Sam Altman names a number that makes the new AI economy tangible: OpenAI's top 'token leader' pushes 100 billion tokens a month through the models — and isn't even the global peak.
stories.quick_take: Sam Altman cited a figure that makes the scale of the new AI economy concrete: OpenAI's internal frontrunner, the so-called token leader, runs 100,000,000,000 tokens through the models every month [1]. And even that isn't the highest consumption worldwide — someone out there uses more [1]. For context, 100 billion tokens is roughly the text volume of hundreds of thousands of books, month after month, from a single instance [1]. That is no longer a human typing and reading; it is a machine autonomously feeding agents, pipelines and workflows [1].

bullets.label: The headline number:
bullets.text: A single top user pushes 100B tokens monthly, and isn't even the global maximum [1].

bullets.label: Books, not chats:
bullets.text: That volume equals hundreds of thousands of books per month from one instance [1].

bullets.label: Conversation to infrastructure:
bullets.text: Usage at this scale means autonomous agents and pipelines, not human prompting [1].

bullets.label: Measured in throughput:
bullets.text: The relevant metric shifts from prompts to industrial token throughput [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: When a lone account consumes books-worth of tokens per minute, AI use has tipped from conversation into industrial infrastructure — and pricing, capacity planning and energy all have to be rethought around throughput [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Sam Altman: 100 billion tokens a month from one user

stories.title: OpenAI's foundation funds the guardrails for the AI era.
stories.toc_summary: The OpenAI Foundation launches 'AI Resilience' with $130M+ in first grants across bio, cyber, model safety and youth protection — part of a pledged $1B-plus.
stories.quick_take: The OpenAI Foundation has launched a program called AI Resilience with more than $130 million in initial grants [1]. The money flows on four fronts: bio-resilience against artificially created pandemics, cyber-resilience for critical infrastructure, model safety to keep human control of the systems, and protection of children and young people from the technology's dark sides [1]. Co-founder Wojciech Zaremba takes the lead [1]. The $130M is only the opener — at least $1 billion is meant to flow over the next year, part of an announced $25 billion commitment [1]. While everyone talks capabilities, the market leader is now funding the guardrails [1].

bullets.label: Four fronts:
bullets.text: Bio, cyber, model safety and youth protection each get dedicated funding [1].

bullets.label: Scale of the pledge:
bullets.text: $130M now, $1B+ over a year, inside a $25B announced commitment [1].

bullets.label: Named leadership:
bullets.text: Co-founder Wojciech Zaremba heads the program, signaling internal weight [1].

bullets.label: Guardrails as strategy:
bullets.text: Funding resilience while rivals tout capabilities is itself a positioning move [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: A market leader bankrolling pandemic, cyber and child-safety resilience reframes 'AI safety' from a research footnote into funded infrastructure — and sets an expectation other labs will be measured against [1].

sources.title: OpenAI Foundation — Resilience in the age of AI

stories.title: An Acemoglu paper models when smarter AI makes us poorer.
stories.toc_summary: Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu's NBER model finds welfare is non-monotone in AI accuracy: past a threshold, ever-better answers can erode the incentive to build new knowledge.
stories.quick_take: MIT economist and Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu, with Dingwen Kong and Asuman Ozdaglar, models the long-run effect of generative AI on human knowledge production in an NBER working paper [1]. The mechanism: solving a hard problem produces two things — the concrete answer and the general principle behind it; if AI hands over the answer, the incentive to work out the principle yourself falls [1]. They call the result a 'knowledge-collapse equilibrium': past an accuracy threshold, people verify, explore and discover less [1]. The formal punchline is that welfare is non-monotone in AI accuracy — beyond a point, rising accuracy can leave society worse off because the capacity for new foundational knowledge erodes [1]. It is a model under assumptions, not destiny, but a serious design question for AI deployment [1].

bullets.label: Two outputs of effort:
bullets.text: Hard problems yield both an answer and a transferable principle; AI supplies the first and weakens the pull toward the second [1].

bullets.label: Knowledge-collapse equilibrium:
bullets.text: Above an accuracy threshold, verification, exploration and discovery taper off [1].

bullets.label: Non-monotone welfare:
bullets.text: More accuracy can reduce welfare past a point — the paper's central, formal result [1].

bullets.label: A design question, not fate:
bullets.text: It is a model under assumptions, framed as an information-design problem for how AI is deployed [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: If ultra-accurate AI quietly starves the human production of general knowledge, the long-run risk isn't bad answers but a thinning stock of new ideas — making how we keep humans exploring a first-order design choice [1].

sources.title: NBER Working Paper 34910 — Acemoglu, Kong & Ozdaglar, 'AI, Human Cognition and Knowledge Collapse'

stories.title: At work, AI is used more for thinking than for producing.
stories.toc_summary: New usage data shows 49% of workplace AI use goes to analysis and decision-making — nearly half — with content creation a distant second.
stories.quick_take: Workplace AI is, above all, a thinking partner rather than an assembly-line worker [1]. According to the breakdown, 49% of AI use at work goes to analyzing, weighing and deciding — almost half [1]. Actually creating work lands a distant second at 19%, followed by interacting with others (17%) and gathering information (15%) [1]. Anyone who thinks of AI only as a text generator is leaving the bigger lever on the table [1]. For companies, the value sits in better decisions, not more output — and teams that deploy AI deliberately as a sparring partner for analysis and judgment strengthen exactly the area that already dominates [1].

bullets.label: Analysis leads at 49%:
bullets.text: Nearly half of workplace AI use is thinking and deciding, not producing [1].

bullets.label: Creation is secondary:
bullets.text: Producing work (19%), interacting (17%) and gathering info (15%) trail well behind [1].

bullets.label: Bigger lever missed:
bullets.text: Treating AI as a mere text generator overlooks its dominant decision-support role [1].

bullets.label: Value in judgment:
bullets.text: Returns come from better decisions; teams should aim AI at analysis and judgment [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: Point your team's AI at the work that already dominates usage — analysis, options and decisions — rather than just drafting, and you reinforce where the measured value actually is [1].

stories.title: China puts 100+ robots on traffic duty at intersections.
stories.toc_summary: In another Chinese city, robots take over traffic duty — conservative estimates put 100+ units already securing roads and keeping lanes clear in regular operation.
stories.quick_take: In a further Chinese city, robots are taking over traffic duty [1]. Conservative estimates put more than 100 units already securing road traffic nationwide and keeping lanes clear [1]. What is still future music elsewhere runs there in regular operation [1]. stories.quick_take: Construction software was a discipline of its own for decades: modeling a part meant months learning menus, constraints and geometry logic [1]. editorial.title: The week agents stopped being a feature and became the platform
editorial.intro: For two years the AI story was a better answer in a chat box. This stretch of news is about something else: the scaffolding for autonomous agents being poured all at once, in silicon, operating systems, search and capital.
editorial.body: Look at what shipped together. Microsoft framed an operating system, Project Solara, around agents instead of apps. NVIDIA pushed CPUs and an open humanoid blueprint built for swarms of them. Perplexity rebuilt search so an agent can call it in a single block of code. And Sam Altman casually noted that one user already runs 100 billion tokens a month — books-worth of throughput from a single instance that no human is typing. Each of these only makes sense if you assume the customer is increasingly a machine acting on someone's behalf. At the same time, the soft infrastructure caught up: Washington turned its AI doctrine into a signed executive order, Florida dragged an AI maker into product liability for the first time, and the OpenAI Foundation started funding resilience as if the guardrails were now part of the build. Even the contrarian signals fit the pattern — Acemoglu's model warning that ever-better answers could erode our incentive to learn, and a usage breakdown showing humans already lean on AI most for judgment, not output. The cheap, conversational phase is closing; the expensive, autonomous, regulated phase is opening.
editorial.pull_quote: The customer, increasingly, is a machine acting on someone's behalf.
editorial.outro: None of this guarantees the agent economy arrives on schedule or pays for the IPO wave now forming behind it. But the direction is unambiguous: the industry is building for throughput and autonomy, and the rules, lawsuits and safety money are arriving to meet it.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: Stop evaluating AI as a smarter chatbot and start asking how your work, tools and risks change when the primary user is an autonomous agent — that is the world the silicon, the OS makers and the regulators are now building for.
